Title: Bitwarden / Vaultwarden
Summary: Vault passwords and SSH keys, with GUI setup and sign-in.
Keywords: vault hasla passwords sejf CLI bw plugin MFA ssh key klucze rsa ed25519

Sections.Title: Initial setup
Paragraphs: Enable Bitwarden / Vaultwarden in Settings → Plugins. The official OSS client is included in a complete ServerDesk package; no CLI installation or file selection is needed. Choose Bitwarden US, Bitwarden EU or Custom server, then enter the HTTPS address and account email.

Choose Save and connect to vault. Settings are saved before opening sign-in. Enter your master password in the masked field. Enter authenticator, email or YubiKey OTP codes in a separate dialog. Select a method configured on your account. A new device may require another email code.

After sign-in, use the vault dialog to sync or sign out. ServerDesk keeps a separate profile per server and email and does not change the Bitwarden app or browser account. The unlock key stays in memory until ServerDesk closes, you select Lock vault, disable the plugin or change accounts. Closing this dialog keeps the session. Unlock vault when ServerDesk starts is available in plugin settings; Skip lets you unlock later.

External client and legacy configuration is an advanced option for an existing CLI. Its executable and data directory are preserved. Configure a shared profile yourself; ServerDesk does not change its server or sign it out. Complete packages support Windows/Linux x64; reinstall the full package if the component is missing or damaged.

Sections.Title: One-time selection and bindings
Paragraphs: When connecting, choose Password from Bitwarden / Vaultwarden. Enter the master password in the masked field, unlock the vault, search by item name or address (at least 2 characters), select a result and choose Use password. Search shows up to 100 Login items.

The dialog first shows Unlock your vault, then Choose an item. Search appears after unlocking, when a valid connection address is searched automatically. Results show the item name and a labeled username. Editing the query clears the previous selection. First-time vault setup in settings and the picker explains three preparation steps; Vault setup details contain the details. Help works offline. Check again retries the CLI status check.

Enter in the password field unlocks the vault; Enter in search finds items. Arrow Down focuses the results, Enter in the list accepts the selection, Ctrl+F returns to search, and Esc closes the dialog. In narrow windows buttons stack below the input fields.

In the connection editor choose Bind vault item. The selected username is filled into the form; review it before saving. Profiles store only item/account/server identifiers and the item name. Connecting reuses the current unlock and reads the current password for that exact item. For SSH private-key authentication, the item password is the passphrase for your selected local key.

The password is used for the username in the profile; a different item username requires confirmation. Bound connections show Change vault item and Remove vault binding. Removing the binding requires saving the form and leaves the vault item intact. Unbound connections show Bind vault item. Profile duplication and configuration export/import omit bindings. Database backups preserve them as profile metadata.
On Windows, vault passwords work with RDP in In ServerDesk tab mode. The external mstsc client uses its own credentials; the editor preserves the binding but disables choosing one in that mode.

Sections.Title: SSH key from vault
Paragraphs: Create or import an SSH Key item in the vault and run bw sync in your CLI. In the SSH connection editor select SSH key from vault as the authentication method, enter the server username, choose Bind vault item and save. The list shows only keys and their fingerprints; binding does not fetch the private key.

When connecting, unlock the vault and choose Use key. RSA 2048–8192 and Ed25519 are supported in OpenSSH, PEM or PKCS#8 format without additional key encryption. Import a key with its own passphrase into Bitwarden first. If the item includes a public key or fingerprint, ServerDesk checks that it matches the private key.

The terminal, SFTP, transfers and monitoring use the key without a temporary key file. Its buffer stays in the active session's memory and is cleared on termination, error or close. Reconnecting fetches the item again; the master password is required only if the vault was locked. SSH host-key trust is confirmed separately.

Configuration export/import omits the vault binding while preserving the authentication method; choose a key again when connecting. Duplicating opens an unbound editor draft; select a key before saving the copy. Older application versions do not support this method. Disabling the plugin preserves the running session but blocks new connections using a vault key.

Sections.Title: Security and limits
Paragraphs: The master password, session key and retrieved password are not automatically copied to the clipboard or saved in the database or logs. CLI search returns decrypted results; the plugin retains only metadata and reads the password for the selected ID. Decrypted data exists transiently in process memory; this does not protect against malicious code running as the same user.

Closing the dialog cancels its pending processes but keeps the unlock. Closing ServerDesk, Lock vault, disabling the plugin or changing account configuration forgets the session key. Sign out of vault account affects only the owned ServerDesk profile; saved bindings remain. External profiles are never signed out. Disabling the plugin preserves data and active SSH/SFTP sessions. Factory reset retains account cache and recovery copies; it is not a secure wipe. Sign out before removing configuration.

The plugin reads Login passwords and SSH Key items; it does not edit the vault or fetch TOTP, attachments or SSH certificates. Use Sync vault explicitly. SSO/FIDO2 and personal API-key primary sign-in are not supported by the GUI. If Bitwarden requests an extra client_secret check during email sign-in, use the masked dialog. HTTPS with a trusted certificate is required; TLS checks are never bypassed. The client may fetch public Bitwarden configuration on first launch. Validate your server using a separate test account.

Title: Getting started
Summary: Add a server, open a session and find the main features.
Keywords: start installation help pierwsze kroki pomoc quick connect szybkie

Sections.Title: Your first connection
Paragraphs: 1. Choose + or New connection. Enter a name, protocol, address and username. For Serial, choose a device instead of a network address. Save the profile.

2. Double-click the profile in the connection tree. Enter the required credentials. Before trusting an SSH host key or RDP certificate, compare its fingerprint with information obtained independently from the administrator.
3. The session opens in a tab. Tabs restored at startup wait for Connect; restoring a tab does not automatically sign in to the server.

Sections.Title: Finding your way around
Paragraphs: The left rail opens connections, favorites, recent sessions, transfers, network tools and enabled plugins. Help and Settings are at the bottom. The Menu in the top-right corner contains additional actions.
Ctrl+Shift+P opens the action palette. Help works offline, searches article contents and lets you copy a topic. Opening Help again returns to the same tab.

Sections.Title: Quick connection
Paragraphs: Menu → Quick connection accepts addresses such as ssh://login@host:22, rdp://host:3389, vnc://host:5900 or serial://COM3?baud=9600. A Linux serial device can use serial:///dev/ttyUSB0?baud=115200.
Check the destination preview before Connect. Edit as profile opens the editor to save the configuration. Do not put a password in the address: enter it in the credentials dialog.

Title: Connections, folders and tags
Summary: Organize profiles, apply filters and change the list order.
Keywords: profiles connections folders tags sorting icons colors polaczenia tagi foldery sortowanie

Sections.Title: Finding a session and expanding folders
Paragraphs: Right-click a saved session tab and choose Show server in connection list, or use that action in the palette. Filters are cleared, the sidebar opens and the saved profile's ancestors expand. Quick/deleted profiles cannot be saved or recreated by this action.

Expand all folders and Collapse all folders are in the Connections area menu and action palette. Normal folder state survives restart. Changes made while searching remain temporary; collapsing moves a hidden selection to its visible root folder.

Sections.Title: Organization and search
Paragraphs: A connection can belong to a folder and have its own color, icon or imported image. A folder's context menu lets you change its icon. Use the star to add a server to Favorites.

Right-click a blank part of the list or the Connections header to add a root-level connection, create a folder, open Quick connection, import/export configuration or clear filters. Right-clicking a server or folder shows actions for that item. New connection in folder prefills the chosen folder. The search box keeps its text-editing menu.

Search includes the name, address, username, folder, description and tags. The protocol filter works together with search. Choose sorting by name, address, protocol or last connection, then select the sort direction.

Sections.Title: Tags and deleting a profile
Paragraphs: In the connection editor, under Organization → Tags, add labels with Enter or +. You can paste multiple names separated by commas or semicolons. Tags in the connection sidebar opens shared colors and Any, All or Untagged filtering. Apply confirms the changes; Cancel discards them.

Deleting a saved connection removes the selected profile, then cleans up its saved credentials. It does not delete remote files, private keys or other profiles. History entries may remain available for reference; they do not recreate the deleted connection.

Title: SSH and the terminal
Summary: Sign-in, host keys, clipboard and reconnecting.
Keywords: terminal ssh password key host fingerprint authentication haslo klucz polaczenie

Sections.Title: Connecting securely
Paragraphs: Set the SSH address, port, username and authentication method in the profile. Check the host-key fingerprint on the first connection. A changed key blocks the connection; do not remove trust until you understand why it changed.

Remembering a password is optional. If the system vault is unavailable, you can use a password for the current session only. Terminal contents are not instructions to ServerDesk: commands you enter run in the remote shell.

Sections.Title: Working and recovering from a lost connection
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Shift+C — copy selected text.
Ctrl+Shift+V — paste into the terminal.
Ctrl+C — shell shortcut, such as interrupting a command.
Set the terminal appearance, font, cursor and scrollback under Settings → Terminal.

After a connection is lost, use Reconnect in the same tab. Read the error reason: TCP refusal, DNS failure, timeout and authentication rejection describe different problems. An authentication rejection alone does not prove that the password is wrong.

Title: SFTP and file transfers
Summary: Two file panels, the transfer queue, editing and safe retries.
Keywords: sftp files upload download transfers editor pliki transfery edytor

Sections.Title: Long filenames and changed sources
Paragraphs: Downloads use a short sibling .serverdesk-UUID.part file, avoiding an oversized temporary filename when the destination name is long. The completed file replaces the destination only after a successful transfer.

Detected source size/write-time changes stop publication and preserve the previous destination. Wait for the source to finish saving and Retry. Metadata checks are not a snapshot or content checksum; same-size/same-timestamp writes, coarse clocks and races can escape detection.

Sections.Title: Browsing files
Paragraphs: Choose SFTP in an SSH tab. Clicking a panel selects the local or remote side. Double-click opens a directory.

Enter — open a directory.
Alt+↑ — go to the parent directory.
Ctrl+L — select the active panel's path.
Ctrl+F — focus the active panel's filter.
Ctrl+Shift+C — copy full paths of selected files.
F5 — refresh the active panel.
Ctrl+A — select visible entries.
Escape in the list — clear selection.
Escape in the filter — clear it and return to the list.
Ctrl+click adds entries to the selection; Shift+click selects a range.

Sections.Title: Copying names and paths
Paragraphs: In the list menu or Actions → Copy to clipboard, choose selected names, full paths or the open directory's path. This is plain text without shell quoting, not a file transfer. The .. entry is skipped and symbolic links copy their own path.

Copying also works with a cached view after connection loss. An unconfirmed path, loading or pending filtering blocks stale selections. An oversized set is rejected before changing the clipboard; select fewer entries.

Sections.Title: Transferring and editing text
Paragraphs: Upload, Download or dragging files creates transfer jobs.

Choose the default text editor under Settings → SFTP. Editing a remote file downloads a local copy. Upload it explicitly after saving changes: saving in the editor does not update the remote file automatically.

Sections.Title: The queue and file operations
Paragraphs: The Transfers sidebar collects SFTP jobs from open SSH tabs, not RDP clipboard operations. Transfer details shows the full state and paths as they were when opened. You can cancel a job, retry a failure or clear finished history. History disappears when the session tab closes.

Retry starts a file from the beginning and requires fresh overwrite consent. If SSH was lost, reconnect the session first. Deleting files or directories is permanent and needs separate confirmation. Normal directory transfers skip symbolic links; copying a link's contents is a separate action.

Title: RDP remote desktop
Summary: Embedded mode, certificates, keyboard and file clipboard.
Keywords: rdp remote desktop freerdp xwayland clipboard certificate dpi pulpit schowek certyfikat

Sections.Title: Windows and Linux
Paragraphs: Set the address, port, username and desktop options in the RDP profile. Windows supports an embedded ServerDesk tab or an external client. Linux embeds an installed X11 FreeRDP client; Wayland sessions also require XWayland.

Enter the password in a masked ServerDesk dialog. NLA and certificate verification remain enabled. On Windows, the system may handle certificate warnings. On Linux, compare SHA-256 before choosing Trust in this tab. That consent does not create a permanent system trust entry.

Sections.Title: Keyboard
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Alt+← — return keyboard focus to ServerDesk.
Ctrl+Alt+→ — return keyboard focus to ServerDesk.
Ctrl+Alt+End — open the remote Windows security screen.
Clipboard redirection and Windows shortcut handling depend on profile settings and remote system policies.

Sections.Title: Dropping files into RDP on Windows
Paragraphs: Enable the RDP clipboard and sign in. Drop local files or folders directly onto the visible desktop or the file area of an open folder in remote Explorer. ServerDesk prepares the files and automatically invokes paste at the drop location.

Do not drop onto the taskbar, application icons or text fields. This copies through the RDP clipboard; remote Windows handles progress, completion and filename conflicts. A paste-submitted message does not confirm transfer completion.

Alternatively, drop onto Files → RDP clipboard or use Choose files, then paste with Ctrl+V in the remote folder. The set must be smaller than 2 GiB. Dropping files onto the RDP desktop on Linux remains unavailable; use a shared folder configured in the profile.

Sections.Title: Files from RDP to this computer
Paragraphs:
1. Copy files or folders in remote Explorer with Ctrl+C.
2. Choose Files from RDP and check the list.
3. Drag the handle below to a local folder or the desktop.

This is a Windows clipboard bridge, not a continuous drag starting in remote Explorer. The clipboard is shared by tabs and applications. After it changes or the session disconnects, copy the files again and refresh the list. Copying leaves the source files on the server.

Available for embedded RDP on Windows. The destination handles saving, conflicts and progress; a drop-submitted message does not confirm copy completion. Ordinary Ctrl+V in local Explorer remains an alternative.

Sections.Title: Checking and reconnecting
Paragraphs: Check server reads availability and TLS information without signing in. A reachable port does not confirm valid credentials or a successful session.
Linux uses manual reconnection; Windows retry options are in the profile.

Title: VNC and serial ports
Summary: A VNC desktop or a terminal for a COM or /dev/tty… device.
Keywords: vnc serial com tty baud port szeregowy

Sections.Title: VNC
Paragraphs: Select VNC, the address and port (5900 by default), and either a VNC password or explicit no-authentication mode. The desktop opens in a tab with mouse, keyboard and scaling support.

Ctrl+Alt+← — return focus to the application.
Ctrl+Alt+→ — return focus to the application.
The Ctrl+Alt+Del button sends that combination to the remote desktop.

Standard VNC does not encrypt traffic. Use a trusted network, VPN or an already established tunnel. TLS/VeNCrypt, system-account authentication, VNC clipboard and VNC file transfers are not currently supported.

Sections.Title: Serial
Paragraphs: Choose the port, such as COM3 or /dev/ttyUSB0, baud rate, data/stop bits, parity and flow control to match your device. You can detect a port or enter it manually. DTR and RTS are off by default.

Connect opens the device terminal; Disconnect releases the port. On Linux your account needs access to that device. If it is busy, check other terminal programs; do not change permissions across the whole system merely to bypass an error.

Title: Tabs, panels and docking
Summary: Up to four panels, floating windows and restoring the layout.
Keywords: workspace tabs split dock layout panele okna podzial dpi

Sections.Title: Arranging your workspace
Paragraphs: Layout offers one panel, two side by side or stacked, three panels (1 + 2), and four panels (2 × 2). Drag the separators to change proportions, or choose Equalize panel sizes.

Drag a tab to another panel or use its context menu. Detach to a separate window moves the tab; closing the floating window docks it back. Help uses the same mechanism so you can read instructions beside a terminal.

Sections.Title: Switching tabs
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Tab — next tab in the active panel.
Ctrl+Shift+Tab — previous tab in the active panel.
Ctrl+Shift+L — list open tabs with search.

Sections.Title: Restoring at startup
Paragraphs: Settings → Workspace contains options for tabs, panels, the sidebar and the startup layout.
The saved layout does not contain passwords or terminal contents. Restored sessions wait for Connect. Help itself is not a saved server session; open it again from the menu when needed.

Title: Appearance, language and settings
Summary: Themes, custom accent, density and module preferences.
Keywords: settings appearance themes language accent font ustawienia jezyk kolory motywy

Sections.Title: Personalizing the interface
Paragraphs: Settings has a search field and Appearance, Terminal, SFTP, Workspace, Monitoring, Security and Plugins categories. Search also accepts text without Polish diacritics.

Appearance offers themes, accent color, font and text size, spacing and corners. Theme and accent changes have live previews. An empty accent value restores the theme color; Cancel rolls back the preview. The terminal palette is configured separately.

Sections.Title: Saving and language
Paragraphs: Save applies your preferences. Changing the language requires restarting; the notice uses the selected language and lets you restart the application. Restart disconnects sessions and stops running operations after confirmation.

Some preferences apply to the next session or startup: read the description beneath the field. Default settings fills the dialog with defaults; Save applies them and Cancel discards them. Saved connections remain intact.

Sections.Title: GitHub updates
Paragraphs: In Settings → Security → Application updates or About, choose Check for updates. From 0.45.1 startup checks are on by default; saved opt-outs are respected. Setting changes apply after Save at the next startup. Choose Update, Skip this version or Remind me at next startup. Skipping hides only that exact release; manual checks remain available. The source is daman11/ServerDesk on GitHub. Profiles and passwords are not sent.

Windows x64 Setup installations can download a SHA-256-verified installer and install after you confirm session closure. A database backup is created. The app restarts after installation. ZIP and Linux copies require manual updates from Releases. SHA-256 does not replace Authenticode; Windows can still report an unknown publisher.

Title: Plugins: monitoring and commands
Summary: Enable extras and use command templates with care.
Keywords: plugins commands cheatsheet linux monitoring komendy sciagnawka

Sections.Title: Enabling plugins
Paragraphs: Settings → Plugins independently enables Linux monitoring and Commands. Changes apply after Save, without restarting. Disabling a plugin preserves its preferences and custom commands and does not disconnect the terminal or SFTP.

Monitoring reads real data over a separate SSH channel without an agent or sudo. The first CPU value requires another sample. Some details depend on commands available on the remote Linux system; polling is reduced in inactive panels.

Sections.Title: Commands
Paragraphs: Open Commands from the rail or Ctrl+Shift+K. Choose a system profile, search a description or command, and use category and risk filters. Clicking a card opens details, parameters, the preview and guidance. You can store your own templates.

In details, use the arrows or Alt+Left/Right to browse neighboring commands in the current results. The counter shows your position. Toggling a favorite keeps the current form while the command and context remain unchanged. Moving to another command starts its own form.

Before inserting or running a command, check the active server and full preview. Action availability depends on the session and context. Execution is a separate explicit action: viewing a list or details does not run commands. Do not put secrets in template names or descriptions.

Sections.Title: Guides and tool options
Paragraphs: Commands → Guides contains 14 mini guides and 168 option/syntax descriptions for 22 tools. Choose Mini guides or Tool options, a system and a query. Topics include SSH keys on Linux/Windows, IP/DNS configuration, logs, services, Docker and disk usage. Steps show configuration files, examples and risk; Copy example never sends anything to a session.

Open ls and search for -a, -A or an option's meaning. Linux short options are case sensitive. Each reference states its scope, such as GNU ls rather than the PowerShell ls alias. Expandable references also appear in matching built-in command details. They never modify the preview or parameter form.

Official documentation → Refresh documentation downloads current text from the selected publisher on demand. Its cached copy and check date work offline; failure or cancellation preserves the previous copy. Opening the panel downloads nothing. Open website shows the complete original in your browser. Long text is excerpted and the publisher's version may differ from your server.

Guides and option tables are reviewed content shipped with the application. Refreshing documentation does not automatically update them or change executable templates. Downloaded text is never run. Disabling the plugin cancels downloads and preserves copies; full factory reset removes the active cache while preserving the pre-reset database backup.

Title: Network tools
Summary: Diagnose a target without creating a server profile.
Keywords: network ping mtr trace dns tcp ports wake wol http tls subnet snmp diagnostyka siec

Sections.Title: Choosing a tool
Paragraphs: Network tools on the left rail offers Ping, Network trace / MTR, DNS queries, TCP port scanner, Wake-on-LAN, HTTP client, TLS inspector, Subnet calculator and SNMP browser.

Enter the target and options in a tab, then choose Start. Stop cancels running work. History and result export are available. A server's menu can pass its address to a tool; opening a tab does not start diagnostics.

Sections.Title: Interpreting results and protecting data
Paragraphs: A missing Ping reply or trace hop may mean ICMP filtering rather than a server failure. An open port confirms TCP service, not a successful login. Run diagnostics only against targets you are authorized to check.

URLs, HTTP headers, responses and results may contain private data. Dedicated secret fields are protected, but always review contents before copying or exporting. The subnet calculator works locally; network tools contact the selected target only after you start them.

Title: Passwords, trust and privacy
Summary: Where data is stored and what trust prompts mean.
Keywords: security privacy credentials password dpapi secret service kwallet bezpieczenstwo hasla dane

Sections.Title: Data and credentials
Paragraphs: On Windows, application data defaults to %APPDATA%\ServerDesk; saved credentials use DPAPI protection for the current Windows account. On Linux, data is in $XDG_DATA_HOME/serverdesk (normally ~/.local/share/serverdesk) and configuration in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/serverdesk.

Linux uses secret-tool and an unlocked Secret Service. Having secret-tool installed does not by itself mean a working vault. KWallet needs to expose the Secret Service interface. If saving is unavailable, use the password without saving or unlock the system vault.

Sections.Title: Trust and sharing information
Paragraphs: SSH host keys and RDP certificates identify the server. Compare fingerprints through an independent channel; do not accept an unexpected change just to connect more quickly. Local password encryption does not replace protecting your operating-system account.

ServerDesk sends no telemetry. Manual and optional startup update checks contact GitHub, which receives your IP and request metadata, without profiles or passwords. Logs do not record terminal contents, but may contain paths and infrastructure details. JSON configuration exports exclude passwords but include profile names, addresses and other metadata: review them before sharing.

Title: Backups, import and reset
Summary: Protect configuration and distinguish the two kinds of reset.
Keywords: backup restore import export reset defaults kopia kopie przywracanie fabryczne

Sections.Title: Backups and moving connections
Paragraphs: Settings → Security → Database backups lets you create a backup, inspect saved files and choose Check backup. Verification checks SQLite, required tables and saved profile validity; it does not restore the database or confirm access to secrets or every history/settings value. Database snapshots are not separate backups of the operating-system credential vault.

Menu → Export configuration creates JSON profiles and folders without secrets. Import creates new IDs and does not attach existing local passwords to the new profiles. Check the imported configuration before connecting. For manual database recovery, close the application and preserve your current data first.

Sections.Title: Default settings and factory reset
Paragraphs: Default settings only changes the preference draft in the dialog. It does not delete profiles. Choose Save to apply those values or Cancel to keep the previous preferences.

Factory reset is a separate confirmed operation. At the next startup it creates a verified database backup, then clears connections, folders, history, SSH trust and plugin data. Earlier backups, logs and external files are retained. Protected vault entries may remain for local recovery; reset is not a secure erasure of all system secrets.

Title: Troubleshooting and logs
Summary: Read the error reason and prepare a useful issue report.
Keywords: troubleshooting logs timeout tls nla error blad logi odrzucono odmowa

Sections.Title: Common causes
Paragraphs: TCP connection refused: check the address, port, service and firewall.
Timeout: check routing, VPN and host availability.
DNS error: check the hostname and resolver.
SSH/RDP authentication rejected: check the full username, domain or local account, authentication method and server policy.
RDP TLS/NLA or certificate failure: check the client message and server fingerprint; do not disable verification. FreeRDP on Linux needs an X11 client, plus XWayland under Wayland.
Filesystem errors, missing directories and access denial are different from a rejected login.

Sections.Title: Viewing logs
Paragraphs: Under Settings → Security → Logs and diagnostics, choose Open logs, then select a file.

Ctrl+F — search the preview.
Enter — go to the next match.
F5 — refresh the log list.

A general error dialog shows an Error ID. Copy it and search the log to find the operation, exception types, codes and stack traces. Concurrent failures have separate entries, but do not open several general error dialogs at once.
Large files preview their last 128 KiB. Save log copy exports the full file to your chosen location. Logs roll daily or after reaching 4 MiB; 14 files are retained, not necessarily 14 days.

Sections.Title: Reporting an issue
Paragraphs: Include the time, protocol, reproduction steps and error message. About → Copy information adds version, build and environment details.
Review the log before sending it; do not include passwords, private keys or the entire data folder. The current version is a public beta: limitations also depend on the operating system and server.

Title: Keyboard shortcuts
Summary: Key shortcuts for the application and active panel.
Keywords: shortcuts keyboard keys skroty klawiatura f1 ctrl

Sections.Title: Application navigation
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Shift+N — new connection.
Ctrl+Shift+O — find a saved connection.
Ctrl+Shift+P — action palette.
Ctrl+Shift+L — list open tabs.
Ctrl+Shift+K — Commands (plugin enabled).
F1 — Help (focus in the application interface).
Terminals and remote desktops retain their own F1.

Sections.Title: Tabs and connection sidebar
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Tab — next tab in the panel.
Ctrl+Shift+Tab — previous tab in the panel.
Ctrl+B — show or hide the sidebar outside the terminal.
Ctrl+Shift+B — show or hide the sidebar from the terminal too.
Ctrl+W — close the active tab outside the terminal.
Ctrl+Shift+W — close the active tab from the terminal too.

Sections.Title: SSH / Serial terminal
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Shift+C — copy selection.
Ctrl+Shift+V — paste.
Ctrl+C — shell shortcut, such as interrupting a command.

Sections.Title: SFTP files
Paragraphs:
Enter — open directory.
Alt+↑ — go to the parent directory.
Ctrl+L — select the active panel's path.
Ctrl+F — focus the active panel's filter.
Ctrl+Shift+C — copy full paths of selected files.
F5 — refresh the active panel.
Ctrl+A — select visible entries.
Escape in the list — clear selection.
Escape in the filter — clear it and return to the list.

Sections.Title: RDP / VNC desktop
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+Alt+← — return focus to ServerDesk.
Ctrl+Alt+→ — return focus to ServerDesk.
Ctrl+Alt+End — remote Windows security screen (RDP).
Desktop shortcuts also depend on the operating system and session settings.

Sections.Title: Help
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+F — search documentation.
Escape — clear the query.
Enter — move to topic selection.
↓ — move to topic selection.

Sections.Title: Log viewer
Paragraphs:
Ctrl+F — search the preview.
Enter — next match.
F5 — refresh the log list.
